analysis.one_liner: Strips criminal immunity from presidents and vice presidents and limits the Supreme Court's say over it.
analysis.headline: The No Kings Act, written to overturn the Supreme Court's July 2024 presidential immunity ruling, never got a Senate vote; it sat on the calendar until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court ruled in July 2024 that presidents have broad immunity from criminal prosecution for official acts, Senate Democrats introduced this bill to declare that no president or vice president has such immunity. It would strip the Supreme Court of authority to dismiss criminal cases against presidents over immunity claims and route any challenge to the bill itself through the D.C. federal courts. The bill never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want a president held to the same criminal laws as everyone else; also any prosecutor pursuing charges against a sitting or former president or vice president.

how_it_helps.text: The bill states that no President, former President, Vice President, or former Vice President shall have any form of immunity from federal criminal prosecution unless Congress specifies one [S2].

It directs that courts may not consider whether a president's alleged crime fell within official duties, reversing the framework the Supreme Court set out in Trump v. United States, which the bill's findings call incorrect [S2].

It removes the Supreme Court's power to dismiss an indictment, halt a trial, overturn a conviction, or otherwise terminate a criminal case against a president on immunity grounds, leaving those decisions in the trial courts [S2].

Its findings cite the founders' intent that a president be 'amenable to personal punishment and disgrace,' unlike a king, and quote lower courts holding that no former president possesses absolute criminal immunity [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Sitting and future presidents and vice presidents, who would lose the immunity from criminal prosecution for official acts that the Supreme Court recognized in July 2024. The Supreme Court would also lose jurisdiction over these cases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Presidents, vice presidents, and the Supreme Court

drawbacks.text: The bill strips the Supreme Court of appellate jurisdiction over presidential criminal-immunity questions and channels all constitutional challenges to the bill itself through the D.C. district court and D.C. Circuit, whose decisions would be final and unappealable to the Supreme Court [S2]. Constitutional scholars have questioned whether Congress can constitutionally wall off Supreme Court review this way; a court could find the bill itself exceeds Congress's authority, which is why it includes a severability clause [S2].

Constitutional challenges to the bill would face an unusually high bar: a court would presume the bill constitutional unless shown otherwise by 'clear and convincing evidence,' a stricter standard than ordinary litigation, and facial challenges would be cut off 180 days after enactment [S2].
The bill had no Republican support at all, making it a single-party response to a court ruling involving one major-party candidate, which limited its path even if it had reached the floor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core goal — holding a president to the same criminal laws as any citizen — addresses a real gap created by the Supreme Court's 2024 immunity ruling. But the bill's method is aggressive: rather than simply legislating immunity standards, it attempts to bar the Supreme Court from reviewing those questions at all, which invites a constitutional showdown the bill could well lose, and its truncated deadlines and heightened evidentiary standard for challenges would be controversial even among supporters of presidential accountability.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2024 and placed on the Senate calendar in September, but Senate leadership never brought it to the floor before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Charles Schumer introduced the No Kings Act on August 1, 2024, with 35 original cosponsors, all Democrats or allied independents, in response to the Supreme Court's July 2024 Trump v. United States immunity decision [S1].
Thirty-six senators cosponsored the bill — 34 of the Senate's 48 Democrats and 2 of its 4 independents; no Republican cosponsored [S3].
The bill was read a second time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on September 9, 2024, Calendar No. 494 [S4].
No further action followed; the bill never received a floor vote, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting and future presidents keep the broad immunity from criminal prosecution for official acts that the Supreme Court recognized in July 2024, since Congress never enacted a legislative override. The Supreme Court's ruling stands unchallenged by statute.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Presidents, vice presidents, and their allies

for.name: Charles Schumer
for.role: Senate Majority Leader and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar but never brought it to a floor vote.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Gave the bill no floor time; no Senate Republican cosponsored it and the bill never came up for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 36 cosponsors were Democrats or allied independents — 34 of 48 Senate Democrats and 2 of 4 independents — and not a single Senate Republican signed on, so the bill split entirely by party.

industries.industry: Sitting and former presidents and vice presidents
industries.note: The bill would remove the immunity from federal criminal prosecution for official acts that the Supreme Court granted in July 2024, exposing the most powerful officeholders to the same criminal laws as everyone else. Their interest in keeping that immunity runs directly against the public's interest in equal accountability.

industries.industry: The Supreme Court as an institution
industries.note: The bill would strip the Court of appellate jurisdiction over presidential immunity questions and make D.C. Circuit rulings in challenges to the bill final. The Court's July 2024 immunity ruling would be legislatively nullified.
